ns1:channel.ns1:description: Nature Geoscience is a monthly journal dedicated to publishing high-quality original research papers across all areas of the geosciences. The journal’s content reflects all the disciplines within the geosciences, including studies of the Earth’s climate system, the solid Earth and the planets. Nature Geoscience covers studies based on all the methods used by geoscientists, ranging from field work and numerical modelling on regional and global scales to theoretical studies and remote sensing. Physical, chemical and biological investigations that contribute to our understanding of the Earth system or the planets are all represented.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Persistent contribution of biogenic emissions to lower stratospheric aerosols via global monsoon convections
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 25 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02115-w

Biogenic secondary organic aerosols transported from the troposphere into the stratosphere by global monsoon convection account for approximately 40% of background stratospheric aerosols worldwide, exceeding the contribution from volcanic aerosol injections, according to measurements from nine airborne field campaigns and model analyses.
ns1:item.dc:title: Persistent contribution of biogenic emissions to lower stratospheric aerosols via global monsoon convections

ns1:item.ns1:title: Experimental simulation of water formation on Earth from dry pebble rain
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02118-7

The growth of planets like Earth through the accretion of pebble-sized material may produce water as pebbles settle through a H2-rich atmosphere and FeO reduces to Fe-rich metal and water, according to experiments of mafic lithologies melted in H2.
ns1:item.dc:title: Experimental simulation of water formation on Earth from dry pebble rain
ns1:item.dc:creator: Susmita Garai
Zachary D. Sharp
Peter L. Olson
Anthony M. Gargano

ns1:item.ns1:title: Sudden collapse of submarine volcano drives extreme hazards
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02098-8

Seafloor mapping before and after the catastrophic 2022 Hunga eruption showed that the centre of the volcano collapsed by over 1 km, displacing 8.9 ± 0.1 km3 of material. Geophysical surveys show that the caldera collapse occurred during the climactic eruption, triggering extreme tsunami hazards, a stratospheric eruption plume and the breakage of underwater cables.
ns1:item.dc:title: Sudden collapse of submarine volcano drives extreme hazards

ns1:item.ns1:title: Reduced Asian monsoon influence on Mediterranean summers in a warmer climate
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02091-1

A warming climate may weaken the influence of the South Asian monsoon on Mediterranean summers, as shifting heat and wind patterns reduce its impact on regional weather, according to climate model projections under a high-emissions scenario.
ns1:item.dc:title: Reduced Asian monsoon influence on Mediterranean summers in a warmer climate
ns1:item.dc:creator: Hanzhao Yu
Tianjun Zhou
Zhun Guo

ns1:item.ns1:title: Global carbon dioxide flux into the surface ocean intensified by rain-induced dilution
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02112-z

Climate models that do not consider the influence of rainfall on surface ocean CO2 uptake are underestimating the ocean carbon sink by about 10%, according to a reassessment of rainfall-related dilution on air–sea CO2 fluxes.
ns1:item.dc:title: Global carbon dioxide flux into the surface ocean intensified by rain-induced dilution
ns1:item.dc:creator: Carson R. Witte
Christopher J. Zappa
Wade R. McGillis

ns1:item.ns1:title: Divergent deep-sea temperatures in the Pacific and Atlantic during the onset of Antarctic glaciation
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02106-x

Deep-sea temperatures in the Pacific Ocean and North Atlantic Ocean responded differently to the expansion of the Antarctic ice sheet at the Eocene–Oligocene transition, according to benthic foraminiferal clumped isotope records.
ns1:item.dc:title: Divergent deep-sea temperatures in the Pacific and Atlantic during the onset of Antarctic glaciation
ns1:item.dc:creator: Victoria E. Taylor
Alison M. Piasecki
Eivind O. Straume
